subject: design-technology
title: Foundations: Thermoplastics vs Thermosets
welcome_lead: Tour a polymer lab and learn the two great families of plastics: thermoplastics and thermosets.
meta_desc: Learn thermoplastics, thermosetting plastics and their key properties.
final_note: You can split plastics into the two families and pick examples for each.

concepts.def: Plastic that softens on heating and can be reshaped.
Plastic that sets permanently once cured.
Long molecule made of repeating monomer units.

walkthroughs.body_html: Thermoplastics have tangled chains that soften when heated and harden when cooled — they can be recycled and reshaped. Thermosets form cross-links during curing that lock the chains; once set they cannot melt again and tend to burn instead.
Key thermoplastics include HDPE and LDPE (bottles, bags), PP (food tubs), PET (drink bottles), PVC (pipes), PS (yoghurt pots), ABS (toys, Lego) and PMMA/acrylic (clear sheet).

walkthroughs.h2: Choosing a plastic for a kettle
walkthroughs.body_html: A kettle needs heat resistance and rigidity. A thermosetting plastic such as melamine formaldehyde or a high-temperature thermoplastic like polypropylene is preferred over PET, which would soften.

mcqs.q: Why can thermoplastics be recycled but thermosets cannot?
options: Thermoplastics are cheaper, so it is worth recycling them.
Thermosets are too dangerous to recycle.
It is the only way to make plastic items.
Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be remoulded; thermosets have cross-links that lock the shape permanently.

mcqs.q: Why is injection moulding suited to high-volume production?
options: It is the cheapest method for any quantity.
Tooling cost is high but per-unit cost is very low at scale.
Current stays the same.
It is the only way to make plastic items.
